title: Dhruva, the star that never moves
hookLine: a five-year-old is pulled off his father's lap, and practices until he becomes the pole star
carry: abhyasa: long, steady, with care, becomes firm ground
tomorrow: Death offers a boy gold, horses and heaven. what does he say?

cards: A small prince, Dhruva, five years old in most tellings, climbs onto his father's lap. His stepmother pulls him off. That seat isn't for you, she says.
If you want it, go pray to Vishnu to be born again as my son. Dhruva runs to his mother in tears. She doesn't tell him to fight back.
She tells him: then go to Vishnu. So a little boy walks out of the city toward the forest. On the way, the sage Narada meets him and gives him a practice: a place to sit, and a name to repeat.

teach.b: Dhruva sits by the river Yamuna and practices.

The Bhagavata counts it out, month by month: fruit every few days, then leaves, then only water, then only air, until by the fifth month he stands on one foot, holding the name, so still the worlds feel it.
And Vishnu comes and stands before him. He gives Dhruva more than a seat on a lap: a place in the sky that never moves.
Dhruva becomes the pole star, the one the others turn around. His name means fixed, firm. Patanjali's threads thirteen and fourteen describe what Dhruva did.
Practice, abhyasa, is the effort to stay steady.
Not the stillness; the effort, the coming back.

teach.h: A LONG TIME, WITHOUT BREAK, WITH DEVOTION.
teach.b: And it becomes firm ground, dridha bhumi, when it's kept up for a long time, without break, and with devotion, satkara: care, reverence, as if it matters.

That's the Hindu teaching on sadhana, daily practice: not intensity, but steadiness and devotion, over years. It's why someone's Nani can sit with the same name on the same mala every morning for decades.
Most mornings feel ordinary. She keeps going anyway, with care.
Patanjali never promises fireworks. He promises ground. And nobody's asking you to stand on one foot.

how: Many Hindus keep a daily sadhana, often japa, repeating a name of God on a mala of 108 beads; children hear Dhruva's story as the boy whose steady devotion made him the pole star, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras cite 1.14 to explain why steadiness matters more than intensity.

o: a perfect sitting with no stray thoughts
the effort of coming back, again and again

games.q: the boy and the three conditions — tap the pairs.
p: gave him a name to repeat

s: Dhruva's mother told him to fight for his father's lap
she told him to go to Vishnu.
thread fourteen names three conditions for a firm practice
a long time, without break, and with devotion.
Patanjali promises you'll feel peaceful every day
he promises firm ground, not daily fireworks.

games.q: your Nani has said the same prayer every morning for decades. by Patanjali and Dhruva, what makes that worth it?
o: the big feelings it gives her each day.
it's kept up long, steadily and with care: that's what makes firm ground.
nothing; one intense retreat would do more.
games.why: a long time, without break, with devotion. Dhruva held one name until he became the star that never moves.

practice: Sit as if someone you respect were in the room, and choose a name or a word: if you pray, Narada's line, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, or simply Rama, or Om; if you don't, a word like peace.
Repeat it softly with the breath, counting on your fingers if you like, the way a mala counts. When you drift, come back, and count the coming back as the practice, not the drifting as a failure.
Nothing needs to happen; you're laying ground.

wordCard.voice: Abhyasa, practice, the effort to return. It becomes firm ground over a long time, steadily, with care, the way Dhruva became the star that doesn't move.

orig.note: Sanskrit: practice, repeated effort; from abhi + as, to apply oneself to something again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: abhyasa, long, steady, with care, becomes firm ground. Dhruva, fixed. Three hundred days, and counting.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 1.13 (tatra sthitau yatno 'bhyasah: practice is the effort to be steady there)

Bhagavata Purana 4.8–4.9 (Dhruva pulled from his father's lap; Narada's instruction and the mantra om namo bhagavate vasudevaya; five months of practice at Madhuvana by the Yamuna; Vishnu grants him the unmoving abode, the pole star)
